title: The 1910 Law That Was Supposed to Keep His Bird in Cape Town Forever
standfirst: In April 2026 the last of Great Zimbabwe's eight sacred soapstone birds finally came home, 137 years after a hunter swapped it for blankets and sold it to Cecil Rhodes. Nobody who actually built the walls it once stood on ever put a name to the work; the men who insisted Africans couldn't have built them made sure of that.

sections.heading: A Sacred Eagle Came Home 137 Years Late
sections.body: On 14 April 2026, officials in Cape Town handed the last of Great Zimbabwe's eight soapstone birds over to Zimbabwe, closing a gap the local press measured to the year: [137 years away](https://www.myjoyonline.com/zimbabwes-iconic-stone-birds-were-taken-by-colonialists-finally-theyre-all-back-home/). The hunter Willi Posselt had cut it from its stone column in 1889 over the armed protest of the people guarding the ruins, paying in blankets and other goods before writing that he meant to "return and secure them from the natives." He sold what he'd taken to Cecil Rhodes, who kept it in the library of his Cape Town estate, Groote Schuur — and it stayed there even after Rhodes died in 1902, because [a 1910 law written to protect his will](https://www.graphic.com.gh/international/international-news/zimbabwes-iconic-stone-birds-were-taken-by-colonialists-finally-theyre-all-back-home.html) barred anyone from selling, letting or transferring anything he had owned. Rather than repeal that law in time, South Africa's government worked around it: it loaned the bird back for two years while the act was reviewed. In Shona it is chapungu, the bateleur eagle, sacred to the Shona and Venda as a messenger to the ancestors. Zimbabwe's president called its return simply ["the return of a national icon"](https://www.zimbabwesituation.com/news/zimbabwe-birds-the-iconic-stone-sculptures-are-all-finally-home-after-137-years/); a Harare archaeology professor called it ["a spiritual homecoming."](https://www.graphic.com.gh/international/international-news/zimbabwes-iconic-stone-birds-were-taken-by-colonialists-finally-theyre-all-back-home.html)

sections.heading: Phoenicians, a Biblical Queen — Anyone But the People Who Lived There
sections.body: In 1871 the German explorer Karl Mauch decided the ruins were the palace of the Queen of Sheba, insisting local Africans had lived in the area for only ["about 40 years"](https://www.worldhistory.org/article/1429/the-impact-of-prejudice-on-the-history-of-great-zi/) and so could not have built them. Twenty years later the archaeologist Theodore Bent, leading a Royal Geographical Society expedition, examined the same soapstone birds and concluded the site had been built by Phoenicians, with Africans only moving in once they had left. Richard Hall went further. Hired by Rhodes's British South Africa Company, he published a book in 1902 crediting the ruins to ["more civilized races"](https://www.worldhistory.org/article/1429/the-impact-of-prejudice-on-the-history-of-great-zi/), then spent his tenure at the site stripping away roughly two metres of its own archaeological deposit — sediment he described in explicitly contemptuous, racial terms — destroying much of the evidence that might have settled the question on the spot.

sections.heading: The Evidence Was In by 1929. The Government Spent Another Fifty Years Denying It
sections.body: David Randall-MacIver's 1905–06 excavation turned up artefacts matching what Shona communities nearby were still making and using, and concluded the ruins were the work of their ancestors. Gertrude Caton-Thompson's more careful stratigraphic dig in 1929 confirmed it, and by the 1950s archaeologists were broadly agreed on [African origins](https://www.worldhistory.org/article/1429/the-impact-of-prejudice-on-the-history-of-great-zi/). None of it changed policy quickly. After Ian Smith's white-minority government declared unilateral independence in 1965, it leaned on researchers directly — one later recalled being told ["the government was pressurising them to withhold the correct information"](https://www.worldhistory.org/article/1429/the-impact-of-prejudice-on-the-history-of-great-zi/) — and tourist guides into the 1970s still showed Black Africans bowing to the white visionaries supposedly responsible. When Black-majority rule finally arrived on 18 April 1980, the new country renamed itself after the ruins: Zimbabwe, most often translated from Shona as [houses of stones](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zimbabwe), though the archaeologist Peter Garlake has argued the older form of the word meant something closer to venerated houses — chiefs' dwellings or graves, not simply architecture.

sections.heading: No Mortar, No Nails — Just Granite That Splits Itself
sections.body: The people who actually built Great Zimbabwe were ancestors of the Shona, probably descended from the [Gokomere culture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Zimbabwe) that had lived on the plateau since around 200 CE, with most construction running from the 11th to the 15th century. They worked without any mortar. Builders heated the faces of exposed granite outcrops and then doused them with water; the thermal shock split the rock into flat slabs along its own bedding planes, ready to be trimmed and [laid in even horizontal courses with no mortar of any kind, held only by their weight and the accuracy of their fit](https://www.studiomatrx.org/architecture-canon/great-zimbabwe), the finished walls battered — sloped gently inward — for stability. The result, the Great Enclosure, has [dry-stone walls up to 11 metres high](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Zimbabwe), still standing eight centuries on. Inside it stands a solid conical tower, nine metres tall, with no door, stair or chamber of any kind; the best guess is that it was [a monumental version of the grain bin, an emblem of a good harvest and of a ruler's power to store and give](https://www.studiomatrx.org/architecture-canon/great-zimbabwe).

sections.heading: Cattle Bought Status. Gold Bought Chinese Porcelain.
sections.body: Great Zimbabwe's wealth rested on cattle, the primary marker of status in its society, and on gold panned from surface deposits and shallow workings across the plateau until those ran out and miners were sinking shafts dozens of metres deep to keep pace. That gold moved east along routes controlled by [Kilwa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kilwa_Kisiwani), the Swahili sultanate that had seized the gold trade of Sofala on the coast and minted coins that have [turned up at Great Zimbabwe itself](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kilwa_Kisiwani). What came back in exchange was ["Chinese Ming porcelain and carved faience from Persia"](https://www.worldhistory.org/Great_Zimbabwe/), glass beads and seashells — none of it made anywhere nearby, all of it dug up at the site. It is the clearest evidence of who was actually paying for Great Zimbabwe: not a named king with a documented treasury, but a trade network reaching to China, run by a city that never needed to leave a receipt.

sections.heading: The Gold Ran Out, the Grass Ran Out, and So Did the City
sections.body: By the middle of the 15th century, ["competition from rival states and the working out of gold deposits are the most likely explanations"](https://www.worldhistory.org/Great_Zimbabwe/) for Great Zimbabwe's decline, compounded by drought and by a population that had overworked the surrounding land for fuel and pasture. Coastal trade ties collapsed within decades. Some Shona-speaking groups [migrated a few hundred kilometres northwards](https://www.worldhistory.org/Great_Zimbabwe/) and founded the Kingdom of Mutapa; others stayed on the plateau and built [Khami](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Khami), 22 kilometres from modern Bulawayo, a city historians read as founded ["at the time of the disappearance of the state at Great Zimbabwe"](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Khami) around 1450. Its builders kept the mortar-less technique but made it their own, terracing walls up to a checkerboard-patterned retaining wall six metres high — proof the method outlived the city that invented it, if not the dynasty that built it.
